chosen_title: You should turn off fans when it's too hot – but how hot is too hot?
caption:
🌡️ Counterintuitive but true: at a certain point, your fan stops cooling you and starts cooking you.

Electric fans work by blowing air across sweaty skin, speeding up evaporation — and evaporation carries heat away from your body. That works brilliantly at moderate temperatures. But once the surrounding air gets hotter than your skin, the fan starts pushing hot air directly at you, sweat evaporates faster than your body can replace it, and your core temperature can actually rise rather than fall.

The exact threshold isn't universal. In dry conditions, published heat research and WHO guidance broadly cite around 35°C (95°F) as the approximate point where fans become counterproductive. Humidity changes the math: in muggy air, sweat evaporates more slowly, so the danger threshold can drop to around 33°C (91°F). Older adults and people on certain medications — diuretics, beta-blockers — sweat less efficiently, meaning their danger zone kicks in even sooner.

Why it matters: heat-related illness kills thousands every year, many of them indoors with a fan spinning. Knowing when to switch to a damp cloth, a cool shower, or air conditioning could genuinely save a life — especially during this summer's record-breaking heat.

Source: New Scientist

slides.headline: Your fan is making you hotter

slides.label: THE STORY
slides.headline: Fans cool you — until they don't
slides.body: Electric fans work by accelerating the evaporation of sweat from your skin, which carries body heat away and leaves you feeling cooler. But scientists explain this mechanism depends entirely on the surrounding air being cooler than your skin temperature. Once temperatures climb high enough, a running fan stops cooling you and instead blasts hot air directly against your body, driving up moisture loss and potentially raising your core temperature — the exact opposite of what you need in extreme heat.

slides.label: HOW IT WORKS
slides.art_prompt: A bold cartoon split-screen scene: on the left half, a cheerful person sits in front of a fan on a mild day — gentle sky-blue sweat-evaporation arrows curl gracefully off their skin into the air and they look blissfully refreshed; on the right half, the same person faces an identical fan on a scorching day but fierce orange arrows blast back from the fan toward them, sweat flying off in sheets like a garden hose, the person dizzy and wilted with spiral eyes — flat cartoon style, lime and white accents, expressive comic characters, no text in image.
slides.headline: Evaporation: saviour or villain?
slides.body: In moderate heat, a fan speeds up evaporation and genuinely cools you down. In extreme heat, that same mechanism turbocharges moisture loss while delivering hot air to your skin — accelerating dehydration with zero temperature benefit.

slides.label: THE NUMBER
slides.caption: The approximate air temperature above which electric fans stop cooling and begin increasing heat stress in dry conditions — a threshold broadly cited in heat health research and WHO guidance; in high humidity, that tipping point can drop to around 33°C (91°F), because muggy air slows the evaporation that makes fans useful in the first place.

slides.label: THE CATCH

slides.headline: Age shrinks your safe window
slides.body: Older adults often have impaired sweat responses, and people on diuretics or beta-blockers sweat less efficiently — meaning the dangerous tipping point arrives at lower temperatures for them than for younger, healthy people.

slides.label: WHY IT MATTERS
points: Fans produce no cold air whatsoever — they cool only by accelerating sweat evaporation, so when ambient air is already hotter than your skin, running a fan simply speeds up dangerous dehydration without lowering your temperature.
Humidity is the hidden multiplier: on a muggy summer day, sweat evaporates far more slowly than in dry heat, which compresses the temperature range in which a fan is actually helpful.

Older adults, people taking diuretics or beta-blockers, and anyone with cardiovascular or kidney conditions have a reduced sweat capacity and face a lower heat threshold — they should not rely on fans alone during extreme weather events.

When a fan stops being safe, the effective alternatives are a damp cloth applied to the neck and wrists, a cool shower, or moving to an air-conditioned space — all of which remove heat from the body through mechanisms that work even when fans don't.
